title: Metrics & SLIs/SLOs
summary: Turning "reliable" into a number you can design around, negotiate with product, and spend deliberately through an error budget.

slides.markdown:
"Make it reliable" isn't a design spec — it's a feeling. **SLIs**, **SLOs**, and error budgets turn reliability into a number you can actually design against: measure something concrete (an SLI), commit to a target for it (an SLO), and use the gap between the target and reality (the error budget) to decide when to ship features versus when to slow down and fix stability.

This topic covers picking good SLIs, setting SLOs that mean something, and spending an error budget on purpose instead of by accident.

slides.sectionTitle: SLI, SLO, SLA: the difference and why it matters
slides.markdown:
An **SLI** (Service Level Indicator) is a measurement — "percentage of requests served in under 200ms." An **SLO** (Service Level Objective) is an internal target for that measurement — "99.5% of requests under 200ms, measured over 28 days." An **SLA** (Service Level Agreement) is an external, often contractual, promise with consequences — "99.9% uptime or you get a service credit."

The distinction matters because they serve different audiences: SLIs are what you instrument, SLOs are what your team designs and operates against, and SLAs are what legal and sales negotiate — usually looser than the internal SLO, so there's margin before a breach becomes a real business problem.

Conflating an SLO with an SLA is a common interview slip — treat the SLO as the tighter, internal bar.

slides.sectionTitle: Choosing good SLIs: latency, error rate, availability, throughput
slides.markdown:
A good SLI measures something the **user directly experiences**, not something convenient to instrument. The usual four: **latency** (how long a request takes, usually p50/p95/p99 rather than average), **error rate** (fraction of requests that fail), **availability** (fraction of time the service can serve requests at all), and **throughput** (requests handled per second, relevant when capacity itself is the risk).

A weak SLI looks measurable but doesn't track user pain — "CPU usage under 80%" says nothing about whether requests are succeeding. A strong SLI for a checkout API is closer to "percentage of checkout requests completed successfully in under 500ms," because that's the thing a real user actually feels.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: an SLO budget burning down over a month
slides.markdown:
![28-day error budget burn-down chart with an incident drop](assets/error-budget-burndown.svg)

An error budget is `1 - SLO` of allowed failure over the measurement window — a 99.5% SLO leaves a 0.5% budget to spend on outages, risky deploys, or planned maintenance. Small day-to-day errors nibble at it steadily; a single incident like day 12 can burn a third of the month's budget in an hour.

Once the budget nears zero, the team's stance should shift from shipping features to protecting reliability — that shift is the entire point of tracking the burn-down.

slides.sectionTitle: Error budgets: turning reliability into a number you can spend
slides.markdown:
An **error budget** is the allowed amount of unreliability implied by your SLO — if the SLO is 99.9% over 30 days, the budget is the remaining 0.1%, roughly 43 minutes of full downtime-equivalent. The budget reframes an argument that's usually emotional ("is it safe to ship?") into one that's numeric ("do we have budget left this month?").

Spending the budget is not automatically bad: a risky deploy, an aggressive rollout, or planned maintenance all consume it deliberately, in exchange for velocity. The failure mode is spending it *accidentally*, through unmonitored flakiness, with nobody noticing until it's gone and an actual incident has no room left to happen in.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: user-facing SLIs vs internal system metrics
slides.markdown:
| | User-facing SLIs | Internal system metrics |
|---|---|---|
| Example | Checkout success rate, p99 API latency | CPU %, queue depth, GC pause time |
| Answers | "Is the user's experience OK?" | "Is this specific component under strain?" |
| Audience | Product, leadership, SLO reviews | On-call engineer, capacity planning |
| Good for alerting on | Symptom-based paging | Root-cause diagnosis, capacity triggers |

**How to decide:** page on user-facing SLIs — they're what the business actually cares about — and use internal metrics as the diagnostic layer you check *after* an SLI alert fires, or as leading indicators for capacity planning before users feel anything.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: an SLO with no teeth — nothing changes when it's breached
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We set an SLO of 99.9%, so we're managing reliability."

**Why it's wrong:** an SLO that nobody checks, with no agreed consequence for breaching it, is decoration. If the team keeps shipping risky changes at the same pace whether the error budget is full or exhausted, the SLO isn't influencing any actual decision — it's a number in a doc.

**Correct model:** an SLO only works paired with a policy — for example, when the error budget is exhausted, feature launches pause until reliability work restores it. The SLO's value is entirely in the behavior change it forces when breached, not in the target itself.
